title: 1 Samuel 20:1–11
context: David flees from Naioth to Jonathan, asking what he has done to provoke Saul. Jonathan at first doubts his father would hide such a plan, but agrees to test Saul during the new moon meal. David proposes a cover story about a family sacrifice in Bethlehem, which the narrative reports without endorsing, and appeals to their ‘covenant of the LORD.’ The two go out to the field to plan. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about honest lament, prudence, and covenant friendship.

verses.text: David fled from Naioth in Ramah, and came and said to Jonathan, “What have I done? What is my iniquity? What is my sin before your father, that he seeks my life?”
verses.arminianNotes:
David flees from Naioth to Jonathan and asks what he has done to make Saul seek his life. His questions are honest.

Arminian readers see David examining himself and seeking an explanation from his friend.
verses.reformedNotes:
David protests his innocence before Jonathan. He cannot find a cause for Saul’s hostility.

Reformed readers see an innocent sufferer bringing his case to a trusted friend, a theme echoed in many psalms. Both traditions read this as shared ground about honest lament.

verses.text: He said to him, “Far from it; you will not die. Behold, my father does nothing either great or small, but that he discloses it to me. Why would my father hide this thing from me? It is not so.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan insists David will not die, since Saul tells him everything. He cannot believe his father would hide this.

Arminian readers see Jonathan’s loyalty to both his father and his friend creating a blind spot.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan trusts his father’s openness with him. He is sincere but mistaken.

Reformed readers see how love can make it hard to see danger clearly. Both traditions read this as shared ground and with sympathy for Jonathan, whose confidence will be tested by what follows.

verses.text: David swore moreover, and said, “Your father knows well that I have found favor in your eyes; and he says, ‘Don’t let Jonathan know this, lest he be grieved;’ but truly as the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David swears that Saul is hiding his intent from Jonathan to spare him grief, and that there is but a step between David and death. The danger is urgent.

Arminian readers see David helping his friend understand the reality.
verses.reformedNotes:
David explains why Saul would keep Jonathan in the dark. His oath underlines his sincerity.

Reformed readers see David honestly naming the danger he faces. Both traditions read this as shared ground, with the vivid phrase ‘but a step between me and death’ capturing his peril.

verses.text: Then Jonathan said to David, “Whatever your soul desires, I will even do it for you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan replies, “Whatever your soul desires, I will even do it for you.” His loyalty is unreserved.

Arminian readers see covenant friendship expressed in willing service. Jonathan holds nothing back from David.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan places himself at David’s disposal. Love moves him to act.

Reformed readers see faithful friendship reflecting covenant love. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground, and Christians often see in Jonathan’s self-giving loyalty a picture of the love Jesus describes in John 15:13.

verses.text: David said to Jonathan, “Behold, tomorrow is the new moon, and I should not fail to dine with the king; but let me go, that I may hide myself in the field to the third day at evening.
verses.arminianNotes:
David proposes hiding in the field during the new moon meal, when he is expected at the king’s table. The plan tests Saul’s intentions.

Arminian readers see practical wisdom in seeking clarity before acting.
verses.reformedNotes:
The new moon was a regular occasion for sacrifice and feasting (Numbers 10:10; 28:11). David’s absence will be noticed.

Reformed readers see David acting prudently under threat. Both traditions read this as shared ground about wise planning in a dangerous situation.

verses.text: If your father misses me at all, then say, ‘David earnestly asked leave of me that he might run to Bethlehem, his city; for it is the yearly sacrifice there for all the family.’
verses.arminianNotes:
If Saul misses him, Jonathan is to say David asked to go to Bethlehem for a yearly family sacrifice. The story is a cover.

Arminian readers note that the narrative reports the excuse without endorsing it.
verses.reformedNotes:
The excuse may not be true; the text gives no sign David went to Bethlehem. Scripture narrates rather than commends.

Reformed readers likewise read it plainly. Both traditions treat the ruse as narrated within a desperate situation, not as a model, and as shared ground.

verses.text: If he says, ‘It is well,’ your servant shall have peace; but if he is angry, then know that evil is determined by him.
verses.arminianNotes:
If Saul says “It is well,” David is safe; if Saul is angry, his evil intent is settled. The test is simple.

Arminian readers see Saul’s response revealing his heart. His reaction will show what he has chosen.
verses.reformedNotes:
Saul’s reaction will function as a sign. David will know the truth.

Reformed readers see God allowing the situation to expose Saul’s intentions. Both traditions read this as shared ground, with the plan designed to bring hidden hostility into the open without immediate danger to David.

verses.text: Therefore deal kindly with your servant, for you have brought your servant into a covenant of the LORD with you; but if there is iniquity in me, kill me yourself, for why should you bring me to your father?”
verses.arminianNotes:
David asks Jonathan to deal kindly with him because of their covenant of the LORD, and to kill him himself if he is guilty. The appeal rests on covenant.

Arminian readers see covenant loyalty as a real obligation freely entered.
verses.reformedNotes:
The friendship is called ‘a covenant of the LORD,’ recalling 18:3. God is its witness.

Reformed readers see covenant faithfulness grounded in God himself. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting the Hebrew idea of steadfast covenant kindness behind ‘deal kindly.’

verses.text: Jonathan said, “Far be it from you; for if I should at all know that evil were determined by my father to come on you, then wouldn’t I tell you that?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan rejects the idea and promises to tell David if Saul intends harm. He reaffirms his loyalty.

Arminian readers see Jonathan’s integrity: he will not betray his friend, whatever it costs him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan answers David’s fear with a promise. He will not hide the truth.

Reformed readers see faithful friendship holding firm under strain. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground, honoring Jonathan’s readiness to place covenant loyalty above family politics and his own prospects.

verses.text: Then David said to Jonathan, “Who will tell me if your father answers you roughly?”
verses.arminianNotes:
David asks who will tell him if Saul answers harshly. Communication is the practical problem.

Arminian readers see David thinking carefully about risks. He needs a safe way to receive word if Jonathan cannot speak to him openly.
verses.reformedNotes:
David’s question leads to the arrow plan. He needs a safe way to learn the outcome.

Reformed readers see prudence within a relationship of trust. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, and both note how the question moves the scene from emotional assurance to practical arrangement.

verses.text: Jonathan said to David, “Come! Let’s go out into the field.” They both went out into the field.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan invites David to go out into the field, and they both go. They seek privacy.

Arminian readers see trust deepening as the friends withdraw to plan together. Privacy protects them both.
verses.reformedNotes:
The move to the field prepares for the covenant renewal that follows. They will not be overheard.

Reformed readers see a solemn setting for covenant promises. Both traditions read this as shared ground, introducing Jonathan’s solemn promises and the plan that follows.
